sharedText: and verily I say unto you
reason: The chapter's top-ranked candidate at its first verse, and it is the discourse marker Christ uses in four verses of this chapter alone (21:1, 21:2, 21:3 with 'verily' doubled, and 21:26). 'Verily I say unto you' occurs in dozens of KJV verses; Luke 13:35 ranked only because the preceding 'and' happens to be there too. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 1:5; listed here because it is the top-scoring row of the chapter and a reader checking the register at 21:1 should be told why it was passed over.

A tempting row, and the temptation is worth recording. 'Give you a sign' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 7:14 — 'Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign' — and 3 Nephi 21:1-7 is a sustained discourse about a sign given by the Lord himself. But the verbal contact will not carry it. 3 Nephi reads 'I give unto you a sign', with the KJV's own commonest dative marker inserted, and 'sign' is otherwise unremarkable; the Book of Mormon uses 'give unto you a sign' at Helaman 14:2 as well, where Samuel the Lamanite announces the birth of Christ, and that verse would be the natural home for an Isaiah 7:14 link if one were to be written. Nothing else of Isaiah 7 is present here: no virgin, no conception, no Immanuel, and no threatened king. Filed rather than written because typology is doing all the work and the wording almost none — the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi is the model.

A five-word run and a genuine KJV singleton — 'harden their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 11:20 — and the senses are exactly opposed, which is what makes it register content rather than noise. In Joshua 11:20 the hardening is God's own act, performed ON the Canaanites so that they will attack Israel and be destroyed without mercy: 'it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly.' In 3 Nephi 21:6 the hardening is the Gentiles' own, it is the thing that must NOT happen, and the alternative offered is repentance, baptism and adoption into Israel. God hardens in order to destroy; the Father waits to see whether they will harden and hopes they will not. The Book of Mormon also uses 'harden their hearts' as a standing idiom throughout, so the singleton is a coincidence of English word order rather than a route.

Recorded because the route exists and the row still fails. 'Shew my power' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 9:17 — Pharaoh raised up 'that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth' — and Romans 9-11 is demonstrably in play in this discourse: 3 Nephi 16:4 draws on Romans 11:25 and 16:10 on Romans 11:22, both adjudicated. Romans 9:17's logic is also 3 Nephi 21:6's logic, that God uses an unwilling nation as the instrument by which his name reaches everyone else. But 3 Nephi reads 'shew forth his power', which is a different construction with a different possessive, and 'shew forth' by itself appears in fifteen KJV verses. Two content words in common is not enough to name a source, and writing the link would be building a verbal case to justify a thematic one.

sharedText: which are of the house of
reason: A six-word run scoring 1.25, and it is a collision of two stock phrases. 'The house of Israel' is the chapter's refrain, in six of its twenty-nine verses (21:1, 21:4, 21:6, 21:7, 21:20, 21:23), and 'which are of the house of' completes it in the ordinary way; 1 Corinthians 1:11's 'them which are of the house of Chloe' is a Corinthian household and has nothing else in common with a covenant made to Israel. The real link at this verse is Ezekiel 24:27, adjudicated.

This one has to be declined explicitly, because Revelation 15:3 is the source of the pilot's flagship link at 1 Nephi 1:14 and 'great and marvellous' is the phrase it supplied. It occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3. But by 3 Nephi it is no longer a borrowing: the Book of Mormon uses 'great and marvellous' twenty-four times across every book, and it is settled corpus idiom long before this chapter. What is genuinely borrowed at 21:9 is Isaiah 29:14's 'a marvellous work among', a KJV singleton, to which the corpus formula has been prefixed as an intensifier. The link is written at 21:9 against Isaiah 29:14 and Acts 13:41; Revelation supplies only the adjective pair, and its adjudication belongs at 1 Nephi 1:14, where it is.

'Cut off from among' occurs in eleven KJV verses, almost all of them the Levitical and Numbers formula for excision from the congregation, and Leviticus 20:17 ranked here on 'they shall be cut off'. The Priestly formula is certainly the ultimate background of the idiom, but it is not the proximate source at this verse and the machine cannot see why. 3 Nephi 21:11's sanction descends by a traceable route: Acts 3:23 reads 'destroyed from among the people'; 1 Nephi 22:20 changed 'destroyed' to 'cut off' and 3 Nephi 20:23 repeated the change; 21:11 inherits it. The link is written against Deuteronomy 18:19 with Acts 3:23 composite and mediation OT-via-earlier-BoM. Leviticus 20:17's own subject — a man who marries his sister — has nothing to do with it.

A cross-reference, filed so that a Hardy row is discharged where a reader will look for it. Hardy's footnote at 3 Ne 21.11 carries the citation 'Mic 5.8-15' alongside Deuteronomy 18:19 and Acts 3:23, on the ground that 'cut off' is the term connecting the Mosaic sanction to the Micah oracle, where it recurs six times. That observation is right and it is taken up in the link written at this verse, but the Micah quotation itself does not begin until 21:12; there is no Micah wording in 21:11 beyond the two words the two passages share. The catalogue therefore writes a link at each of 21:12, 21:13, 21:14, 21:15, 21:16, 21:17, 21:18 and 21:21 against Micah 5:8, 5:9, 5:10, 5:11, 5:12, 5:13, 5:14 and 5:15 respectively, so that each verse of the quotation can be seen doing its own work, and sends a reader from 21:11 to 21:12 for the start of it. Hardy's own convention is to hang a multi-verse citation on one verse of the span, as he does again at 21:13 for Micah 5:8-9.

sharedText: delivered unto the Gentiles and shall
reason: A five-word run, and the sense is inverted in a way worth naming. Luke 18:32 is the third passion prediction: 'he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on'. Christ is the thing handed to the Gentiles, and what follows is his humiliation. In 3 Nephi 21:11 Christ is the speaker, what is brought forth unto the Gentiles is a book, and the power to bring it is given rather than surrendered. The shared string is 'unto the Gentiles and shall', which is grammar. Recorded because the surface pairing of Christ, the Gentiles and a handing-over is exactly the kind of coincidence a reader might mistake for a source.

sharedText: in the midst of them as
reason: Six words, and every one of them is supplied by the verse the Book of Mormon is actually quoting. Micah 5:8 reads 'in the midst of many people as a lion'; 3 Nephi 21:12 reads 'in the midst of them, as a lion'. Isaiah 25:11's Moabite spreading his hands to swim is an artifact of the shortened phrase matching. The link is written at 21:12 against Micah 5:8.

sharedText: for it shall come to pass in that day, saith the
reason: An eleven-word run, the longest non-Micah run in the chapter, and it is entirely the KJV's prophetic dating formula. 'And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD' opens Jeremiah 30:8, Micah 5:10, Hosea 2:16, Zechariah 13:2 and many more; the reason it appears verbatim at 3 Nephi 21:14 is that Micah 5:10 is being quoted, and Micah 5:10 has it. Jeremiah 30:8's content — breaking a yoke from a neck — is not present. Filed rather than passed over in silence only because eleven words is long enough that a reader might wonder.

Five words, and they belong to Micah 5:12, which this verse is quoting almost entire: 'out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers'. Deuteronomy 3:2's 'into thy hand; and thou shalt do unto him as thou didst unto Sihon' is a delivery of an enemy, the opposite transaction. The link is written at 21:16 against Micah 5:12.

The best of several New Testament vice-list candidates and still not a link. 'Envyings' occurs in exactly two KJV verses (2 Corinthians 12:20, Galatians 5:21) and 'strifes' in four, and 2 Corinthians 12:20 is the only KJV verse holding both — 'debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults'. But the two words are not adjacent there, and the four other items in the Book of Mormon's list are not Paul's: 'lyings', 'deceivings', 'priestcrafts' and 'whoredoms', of which 'priestcrafts' occurs in no KJV verse at all. This is the corpus's own recurring vice-list, run at 2 Nephi 26:21, 3 Nephi 16:10, 3 Nephi 30:2, 4 Nephi 1:16 and Alma 16:18 with much the same members; 3 Nephi 16:10, twenty pages earlier in the same discourse, is its nearest neighbour. A catalogue of dependence should not attribute a house formula to the one Pauline verse that shares two of its nouns.

'Shall be done away' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:10, and the eschatological sense there — 'when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away' — sits well with a verse about the vices of the last days being abolished. The count is real and the row still fails, because the phrase is standing Book of Mormon idiom: 'done away' appears in eleven Book of Mormon verses across six books, including three others in 3 Nephi alone (9:19, 11:30, 12:47). A KJV singleton that the corpus has naturalized is evidence about the corpus's English, not about this verse's source. Worth recording in data/kjv-phrases.json as an Index Verborum entry rather than as a link.

'Beloved Son' occurs in ten KJV verses, six of them the voice from heaven at the baptism and the transfiguration, and the speaker at 3 Nephi 21:20 is the Father — so the pairing is not accidental. But it is not new here. 3 Nephi 11:7 is the Father's voice at the theophany that opens this entire visit: 'Behold, my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, in whom I have glorified my name, hear ye him', which is Matthew 17:5 almost word for word, and that verse is where the link is adjudicated. By 21:20 the title is the discourse's established way of referring to Christ in the Father's mouth. The sanction clause of this verse — 'them will I cut off from among my people' — is likewise the second use of 21:11's, and it is adjudicated there.

Five words, and 'the remnant of Jacob' has been in front of the reader continuously since 21:12, where it entered as the opening phrase of the Micah 5:8 quotation. Isaiah 10:21's 'The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God' is a different oracle about a different remnant, and nothing else of Isaiah 10 is present. The word 'unto' completing the run belongs to 'unto whom I have given this land'. The chapter's use of the phrase is adjudicated at 21:12 against Micah 5:8, with 3 Nephi 16:14 in recurrenceRefs.

sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the
reason: A seven-word run and the top candidate at this verse, and it is the Book of Mormon's own dispersion formula, adopted at 1 Nephi 10:12 and used continuously thereafter; the standing exclusion filed in 1 Nephi covers it, and a near-identical entry stands at 3 Nephi 9:1. Ezekiel 34:6 reads 'my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth' and 3 Nephi 21:24 reads 'scattered upon all the face of the land', which is the corpus's habitual substitution. The real intertext of 21:23-24 is the New Jerusalem, adjudicated at 21:23.

'Powers of heaven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:26 — 'the powers of heaven shall be shaken' — with Matthew 24:29's 'the powers of the heavens' and Mark 13:25's 'the powers that are in heaven' beside it. All three are the cosmic collapse of the Olivet discourse, where the shaking of the heavenly powers is a terror preceding the Son of man. 3 Nephi 21:25 is its opposite: 'then shall the power of heaven come down among them; and I also will be in the midst', a descent that constitutes the gathered city rather than dissolving the sky. The first edition also reads the singular 'power', which is in no King James verse at all, though Hardy's apparatus records the plural in the Printer's Manuscript; and the sentence is in any case a restatement of 3 Nephi 20:22, 'the powers of heaven shall be in the midst of this people; yea, even I will be in the midst of you', which is where the phrase enters this discourse.

Five words. Leviticus 25:30 concerns a house inside a walled city that is not redeemed within the year: it 'shall not go out in the jubile', meaning it does not revert to its original owner at the jubilee. The subject is a building and 'go out' is a technical term of property law. 3 Nephi 21:29's 'they shall not go out in haste' is Isaiah 52:12's second-Exodus departure and is adjudicated there. The row is a clean example of the trap named in ADJUDICATING §4 — the window closes one word early, and the next word is 'the jubile'.
